Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 358 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018) 
 
 
Survey Method 
Distance sampling methods were used to determine moose density as described in the Distance Sampling 
Chapter of the Aerial Ungulate Survey Protocol Manual (ESRD, 2014). Transects were 10 km long, spaced 1.2 km 
apart and oriented north-south.  A random sample of the available transects was flown.  
The unit was initially stratified into Agricultural (including a 1000 m buffer) and Forest, however encounter rates 
were very similar between these strata.  Stratification did not enhance the precision of the estimate, and so was 
not included in the final analysis. A minimum total count method was used for elk, combining transect observations 
with additional search effort in areas of traditionally high winter elk density.  
 
Results 
One hundred and forty-seven transects were surveyed on January 19 and 26, 2018 for a total distance survey 
effort of 578 km and 14.6 hours flying time. In total, 242 moose were observed from 150 independent groups of 
moose. Of the 240 moose that were successfully classified, 54 were bulls, 119 were cows, and 67 were calves. Of 
the bulls observed, 70% had already shed their antlers. Of those bulls still with antlers, two -thirds were small (small 
spike or forked antlers) and one third were medium (small palmated antler ‘paddles’). No large bulls (large 
palmated antlers with minimum 3 points to the front with a spread more than half the body length) were observed. 
The bull:cow and calf:cow ratio were 0.45 and 0.57 respectively after adjusting for strata area. T he final density 
estimate was 0.77 moose/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 12%. The estimated moose abundance for WMU 
358 is 2224 (90% CI 1825 - 2710).  
On January 26th and 27th, 2018, we flew an additional 7.0 hrs to locate significant groups of elk in areas of 
traditionally high winter density.  A total of 1206 elk were observed in 42 groups from transects and focussed 
search flights.  Of the 829 elk that were successfully classified, 48 were bulls, 597 were cows, and 184 were 
calves.  Of the bulls observed, 75% were small (1 or 2 point) 23% were medium (3 to 5 point) and only 2% were 
large (six point or greater).  At this time of year, most bull elk still have antlers so these proportions should be 
representative of the population post-hunting season. 
We also observed 109 mule deer and 28 white-tailed deer, however these should not be considered minimum total 
counts as we did not achieve full coverage of the unit searching for these species.
